newsitem.title: GERMANY: Chechen sympathiser admits toy gun hijacking.
newsitem.headline: Chechen sympathiser admits toy gun hijacking.

text.p: A Turkish waiter admitted in court on Wednesday that he had hijacked a plane with a toy gun -- an act he confessed was aimed at winning sympathy for the Chechen separatist cause in Russia.
Ramazan Aydin, 21, pleaded guilty to holding up a Boeing 727 on route from nothern Cyprus to Istanbul with 147 passengers and crew on board and diverting it to Munich last March.
He said that as a devout Moslem he merely wanted to help his "Chechen brothers".

After he surrendered and freed his hostages at Munich airport in March, Bavarian police said he had used a toy gun and duped authorities in several countries for 11 hours into believing three more armed hijackers were also on board.
At the opening day of his trial in the German town of Landshut, Aydin said he had no intention of hurting anyone.

"The lives and health of the passengers was just as important as the lives of my Moslem Chechen brothers," he said, explaining he had hoped his act would prompt European states to intervene to end the conflict in Russia.
Aydin said he and a friend had visited Chechnya, an autonomous republic in southern Russia, without Russian visas on what he described as a "pirate ship" in the summer of 1995.

Speaking in Turkish through an interpreter, he described how they witnessed atrocities committed during the conflict between Russian forces and Chechen rebels and that his friend was later killed in the Chechen capital Grozny.
"I would not hijack a plane today; my attitude to violence has completely changed," Aydin said in his plea. Justice officials said the trial in the town near Munich was likely to last three days.
The court would decide whether Aydin, who was 20 years old at the time of the hijacking, should be tried according to juvenile law.

Around 500 police and security personnel, including members of the crack GSG-9 anti-guerrilla force, raced to Munich airport in March after Aydin ordered the jet to fly to the German city after a refuelling stop in Sofia.

But when they arrived he set no deadlines and asked only to see a human rights lawyer and make a statement on Chechnya. One of the pilots afterwards said that even a petrol bomb he claimed to have was a fake.
Moscow agreed on a truce with Chechen rebels in August and Russian troops, which failed to establish control over Chechnya in 21 months of bloody fighting, have started withdrawing from the region.
